To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the insulin binding capacity of the erythrocytic insulin receptor can be increased by incubating the erythrocytes in vitro with disulfide-reducing agents (such as dithiothriitol or 2-mercaptethanol) and 2) agents which alkylate and/or oxidise free sulfydryl groups tend to decrease specific binding to the erythocytic insulin receptor.
insulin receptor affinity can be modulated by altering the red cell sulfhydryl environment.
the insulin receptor has a sulfhydryl group that is important for its activity and that the activity of the receptor can be increased by reducing this group with a disulfide reducing agent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of disulfide reducing agent on insulin binding to erythrocyte receptors and the role of sulfhydryls in insulin action.
the role of sulfhydryls in the insulin binding site of the insulin receptor.
the effect of various sulfhydryl reagents on the binding of 125-I-insulin to the human erythrocyte membrane receptor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
insulin binding to the insulin receptor is modulated by sulfhydryl group changes.
sulfhydryl reagents affect insulin binding to the receptor in vitro by changing receptor affinity.
the sulfhydryl group is a critical part of the insulin receptor and that its modification by disulfide reducing agent or oxidising agent can alter insulin receptor function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
insulin binding is increased by reducing agents (e.g. dithiothriol) and that this increase is due to an increase in receptor number and affinity.
the insulin binding to the insulin receptor is modulated by a variety of factors, some of which may have clinical significance.
sulfhydryl agents may have important roles in the regulation of insulin binding to its receptor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the reducing agents are not toxic to the red cell.
the reducing agents increase insulin receptor affinity.
insulin receptors are sensitive to changes in the redox state.
